new_statements.quote: However, the evidence presented here shows that while Nkoroo has moved in the direction of an accentual system, Defaka remains a true tone system, with some structural borrowing from Nkoroo. [...] Both Defaka and Nkoroo are two-tone plus downstep languages. [p. 1] [...] Nkoroo noun compounds and pro-clitic+noun host combinations share a fixed tone pattern: they take a uniform HL pattern, except the noun is L-toned, and the entire structure is L. This output tone occurs without regard to the input tone of the noun. [p. 11]

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: VERBATIM CHECK. Opened (extracted text of the 11-page WOCAL 6 handout, text layer present). All three quoted sentences are there verbatim: p. 1 §1 lines 15-17 'However, the evidence presented here shows that while Nkoroo has moved in the direction of an accentual system, Defaka remains a true tone system, with some structural borrowing from Nkoroo.'; p. 1 §2 line 30 'Both Defaka and Nkoroo are two-tone plus downstep languages.'; p. 11 §11 Conclusions lines 493-495 'Nkoroo noun compounds and pro-clitic+noun host combinations share a fixed tone pattern: they take a uniform HL pattern, except the noun is L-toned, and the entire structure is L. This output tone occurs without regard to the inpu…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Nkoroo is described as a two-tone (H, L) plus downstep language whose lexical prosody is tonal; no word stress is described or mentioned. The authors add that Nkoroo is drifting toward an 'accentual' system in the Ijoid sense: nouns keep their lexical tone in isolation and in most phrases, but compounds, proclitic+noun and 'one'+noun units neutralise input tones to a single culminative HL contour (fall after the first syllable of the second element), or all-L when the first element/clitic is L. Whether a syllable is 'stressed' is never at issue.
new_statements.exceptions: Tonal: no HLHL compounds ('If the fall already occurs on the first noun, there cannot be a second fall on the second noun', p. 2); voiceless consonants block H spreading in demonstrative+noun (p. 9); numerals 2-4 and 'some/many' leave the noun's underlying tone unaffected; numerals 5-9 carry a L clitic [a] whose L spreads to the noun's first syllable (p. 8).
new_statements.domain_note: Word- and phrase-level tone of nouns in isolation, noun+noun compounds, proclitic+noun, numeral+noun and demonstrative+noun; data from the NSF documentation project in Nkoroo town (2007-2011). Sentence prosody only via Harry (1987: 72), quoted in the ACAL 40 slides: questions and statements have the same pitch patterns.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted source describes the Nkoroo of Nkoroo town (Opobo/Nkoroo LGA, Rivers State), i.e. nkor1239 itself, which Obikudo (2024: 2509) says 'is referred to as Kirika by its speakers'; Glottolog lists no dialects. It is an Eastern Ijo variety (closest relatives Kalabari, Ibani, Kirike/Okrika) and is the daily language of the Defaka [defa1248] community, whose phonetics Shryock et al. say may be indistinguishable from Nkoroo at that level; Akinlabi & Connell argue the two tone systems remain distinct.

sources.locator: §1 Introduction and §2 Key claims, p. 1; §11 Conclusions, p. 11 (compound/clitic generalisations also §2 p. 3 and §5 p. 7)
sources.note: p. 1: 'Both Defaka and Nkoroo are two-tone plus downstep languages'; 'Nkoroo has moved in the direction of an accentual system'. pp. 3, 6-11: noun compounds, proclitic+noun and 'one'+noun take a uniform HL output pattern regardless of input tones (LL if N1/clitic is L); numerals 2-4 and 'some/many' leave noun tones unchanged; 'no tone spreading in phrases'. p. 11: accentual drift 'now widespread in Ijoid (Williamson 1986)'. The words stress/accent placement never occur; no statement on word stress.
